canonical_topic: Desert Southwest power market and trading hubs
definition: The Desert Southwest is a moderate-winter, hot-summer region that typically runs a generation surplus (mainly natural gas, with some coal and hydro, plus strong solar potential) and exports power to Southern California, trading through three major hubs.
core_idea: Palo Verde (near Phoenix, at a major nuclear plant/switching yard) is the benchmark hub for the northern part of the region and a key gateway to California; Mead (near Las Vegas, at Hoover Dam/Lake Mead) is the primary delivery point for southern Nevada hydropower; Four Corners (northwestern New Mexico) sits at the junction of several major transmission lines.
key_points: Region has moderate winters and long hot summers, usually generation-surplus and a major exporter to Southern California
Natural gas is the most common marginal fuel, given abundant regional reserves; coal and hydropower are also present
Abundant sunlight makes the region attractive for solar generation
Three major hubs: Palo Verde, Mead, Four Corners
Palo Verde: ~45 miles west of Phoenix, at a major nuclear plant/switching yard, hosts many California transmission lines, and is the benchmark for power delivered to Colorado and Wyoming
Mead: outskirts of Las Vegas, at Lake Mead/Hoover Dam, primary delivery point for southern Nevada power
Four Corners: northwestern New Mexico, at the interconnection of several major transmission lines
trading_implications: Palo Verde is the standard benchmark price point for trades into California and the northern part of the Desert Southwest region
